text: The Taliban published an 11-page biography of reclusive leader Mullah Mohammed Omar, seeking to dispel rumors of his death amid years without video or audio proof of life. Analysts say the timing also counters ISIS leader al-Baghdadi's rival claim to Islamic leadership. The document details Omar's biography and daily routine but omits mentions of his alliance with Osama bin Laden and al Qaeda.

Hundreds gathered in South Carolina to mourn Walter Scott, the unarmed black man fatally shot in the back by a white police officer, with speakers calling for racial justice reform. Officer Michael Slager, charged with murder in the shooting, remains jailed, while witnesses and experts debate whether a struggle before the shooting could reduce the charge to manslaughter.

Former TSA agent Daniel Boykin, 33, was sentenced to six months in jail and five and a half years of probation for secretly videotaping a female co-worker in a TSA-only bathroom and repeatedly entering her home to record videos and photos. Police found over 90 videos and 1,500 photos of the victim on his devices, and he pleaded guilty to unlawful photography, aggravated burglary and violating the computer act. Boykin was fired last year when the investigation began.

Cape Verde is leveraging its rich musical heritage, born from a mix of African and Portuguese influences, to boost economic development in the absence of traditional natural resources. Events like the Kriol Jazz Festival and Atlantic Music Expo aim to promote local artists internationally and drive tourism, which is projected to reach 20% of GDP by 2024. Government and private sector figures see music as a cost-effective way to raise the country's global profile.

Arsenal beat Burnley 1-0 thanks to an Aaron Ramsey goal, moving to within four points of leaders Chelsea, who have two games in hand and face QPR next. Coach Arsene Wenger praised midfielder Francis Coquelin as Arsenal extended their winning run to eight games, setting up a crucial title showdown with Chelsea next week. Elsewhere, Aston Villa beat Tottenham, West Brom lost late to Leicester, and Crystal Palace thrashed Sunderland 4-1, with Yannick Bolasie scoring the club's first Premier League hat trick.

Original "Twin Peaks" cast members have launched a #SaveTwinPeaks campaign backing David Lynch after he exited Showtime's revival over a salary dispute. Lynch, who co-created the series with Mark Frost, said Showtime hadn't offered enough money to do the script justice, though the network says it hopes both creators will return. Kyle MacLachlan remains the only cast member currently confirmed for the 2016 reboot.

Andrew Getty, 47, grandson of oil tycoon J. Paul Getty, appears to have died of natural causes, Los Angeles police said, with no foul play suspected. An autopsy is pending; medication was found at his home, though its relevance to his death is unclear. Getty, who had recently sought a restraining order against an ex-girlfriend citing a serious health condition, was one of the heirs to the Getty oil fortune.

Nyia Parler, 41, was taken into custody in Maryland after Philadelphia police said she abandoned her quadriplegic, cerebral palsy-afflicted son in a wooded park for over four days while she visited her boyfriend. The 21-year-old victim, found by a passerby suffering from dehydration, malnutrition and infection risk, is hospitalized; Parler faces aggravated assault and related charges but cannot be extradited until she completes unspecified treatment.

NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer has named an asteroid, 316201 Malala, after Pakistani education activist Malala Yousafzai. Mainzer, who discovered the asteroid in 2010, said she wanted to honor Malala partly because few asteroids recognize women's contributions. The asteroid orbits between Mars and Jupiter every five and a half years.

A gastrointestinal illness outbreak has sickened 100 people aboard the cruise ship Celebrity Infinity, the CDC reported. CDC investigators plan to meet the ship in San Diego on Monday to determine the cause, while Celebrity Cruises has increased cleaning and disinfection efforts. This marks the third such outbreak on the vessel since 2006.

The entire "Star Wars" saga hit digital HD, Mindy Kaling's brother sparked controversy claiming he faked being black for medical school admission, and "Dukes of Hazzard" actor James Best died. Other trending stories included Burger King gifting a free wedding to a couple named Joel Burger and Ashley King, Michelle Obama dancing at the Easter egg roll, and Nina Dobrev's exit from "The Vampire Diaries."

Philadelphia woman Keonna Thomas was charged Thursday with attempting to provide material support to ISIS after allegedly purchasing tickets to travel overseas to join the group, citing social media posts dating to 2013. Two New York women, Noelle Velentzas and Asia Siddiqui, were also arrested this week and accused of plotting to build an explosive device for a domestic attack. Officials say more than 30 similar terror-related cases have been prosecuted in the past 18 months, 18 involving ISIS.

HBO released a teaser for season 2 of "True Detective," premiering June 21 and starring Colin Farrell, Vince Vaughn, Rachel McAdams and Taylor Kitsch. The new season follows a murder investigation involving multiple law enforcement officers and a criminal in California. Season 1, starring Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson, was a hit that crashed HBO Go upon its finale in March 2014.

Carlos Colina, 32, was arraigned Monday on charges including assault and battery causing serious bodily injury and improper disposal of a body after human remains found in a duffel bag in Cambridge, Massachusetts, were traced back to him. The remains, discovered Saturday at two locations, belonged to 26-year-old Jonathan Camilien, who reportedly knew Colina. The next hearing is scheduled for April 14.

Louisville basketball star Trey Moses invited high school freshman Ellie Meredith, who has Down syndrome, to be his prom date, surprising her with flowers and a poster during her P.E. class. The gesture, arranged with Ellie's parents' prior approval, went viral after photos were posted online. Both families expressed pride, with Trey planning to study special education alongside playing college basketball at Ball State.

This week's TV picks include NBC's "A.D. The Bible Continues," a sequel to History Channel's ratings hit, premiering Sunday with Juan Pablo Di Pace as Jesus. Also debuting: the beginning of "Mad Men's" final episodes, new seasons of "Louie" and "American Odyssey," Billy Crystal's mockumentary "The Comedians," and Marvel's "Daredevil" on Netflix.

Indiana Gov. Mike Pence faces backlash for signing a "religious freedom" law seen as enabling discrimination against LGBT people, a move meant to bolster his conservative credentials ahead of a possible 2016 presidential run. Similar bills are advancing in over a dozen states, and potential GOP candidates like Cruz, Huckabee, Jindal and Walker have echoed similar anti-same-sex-marriage stances, ensuring LGBT rights will be a major issue in the primary. Despite growing national support for gay rights, the controversy shows conservative opposition remains a potent political force.

Apple's new mobile OS update introduces diverse emojis, including varied skin tones and same-sex couples, sparking mixed reactions. Critics note omissions like redheads and Armenia's flag, while others debate implications like Santa Claus's potential skin tones. The author argues the update reflects America's changing demographics and hopes society will similarly evolve toward inclusivity.

Singer Avril Lavigne revealed to People magazine that she was bedridden for five months after contracting Lyme disease from a tick bite last spring. The 30-year-old, who says she is now "80 percent better," said she feared she was dying during her illness, which sparked widespread speculation after fan reports of her health struggles went viral.

New research from the Anne Frank House suggests Anne Frank and her sister Margot died in February 1945, at least a month earlier than the previously assumed date of March 31. Researchers based their findings on Red Cross archives and survivor testimonies, concluding the sisters likely succumbed to a typhus outbreak at Bergen-Belsen before March. The exact dates of death remain unclear, though Margot is believed to have died first.

Two Troy University students, Ryan Calhoun and Delonte Martistee, have been arrested and charged with sexual battery for allegedly gang raping a woman during spring break at Panama City Beach, Florida. The alleged assault, which occurred behind a popular bar in March 2015, was discovered on video during an unrelated police investigation in Alabama. Both students have been suspended from school, and more arrests are expected as the investigation continues.

A stray dog named Theia survived being hit by a car, hit with a hammer, and buried, before staggering to a nearby farm four days later. She is now recovering at Washington State University's veterinary hospital, with fundraising efforts surpassing $10,000 to cover her medical treatment.

The FBI confirmed that Malaysian bomb maker Marwan, real name Zulkifli bin Hir, was killed in a January raid in the Philippines and has been removed from its Most Wanted Terrorists list. The mission killed 44 elite police commandos and shattered a ceasefire with rebel group MILF, sparking controversy over whether the operation's focus on Marwan jeopardized the region's peace process.

Republican Rep. Ed Royce criticizes the Iran nuclear framework negotiated by President Obama, arguing it squanders sanctions-driven leverage by letting Iran keep its nuclear infrastructure, lifting billions in sanctions, and letting key restrictions expire after just 10 years. He warns without "anytime, anywhere" IAEA inspections, Iran could cheat as North Korea did, while continuing to fund terrorism across the Middle East.

AMC's "Mad Men" begins its final season, capping eight years chronicling a 1960s ad agency and America's cultural upheaval. As the series picks up after the July 1969 moon landing, speculation swirls about major characters' fates amid the agency's turmoil following its merger and acquisition by McCann Erickson. Creator Matthew Weiner has kept plot details secret, but the show is expected to explore late-1960s events while resolving arcs for Don Draper, Peggy Olson, Roger Sterling and others.

Katie, a giraffe at the Dallas Zoo, gave birth to a six-foot-tall calf on Friday evening in an hour-long labor livestreamed by Animal Planet using 10 cameras. The newborn's gender and condition were not immediately announced, though the zoo reported positive signs including nursing attempts and ear movement. The calf joins Katie's 4-year-old daughter Jamie in the zoo's herd of 12 giraffes.

Loretta Lynch's confirmation as attorney general has stalled in the Senate for over six months, longer than the eight previous nominees combined, despite clearing the Judiciary Committee in February. Supporters, including her father and NAACP activists, suggest race may be a factor in the delay, while Republicans attribute it to unrelated partisan disputes over immigration and a human trafficking bill. Lynch's family and supporters in Durham, North Carolina, continue advocating for her confirmation.

Armed assailants stormed the attorney general's office in Balkh province, northern Afghanistan, on Thursday, killing three people and wounding five, officials said. The dead included two police officers and a security guard. Afghan security forces continued exchanging fire with the attackers while working to avoid civilian casualties, after rescuing most staff and civilians.

Bob Barker, 91, returned to "The Price Is Right" on April 1 for the first time in eight years, hosting the show's first game before handing duties back to current host Drew Carey. Barker had hosted the program for 35 years until stepping down in 2007.

B.B. King, 89, was hospitalized for dehydration caused by Type II diabetes but was released the same day. The legendary blues guitarist is resting at home with his grandchildren. He suffered a similar dehydration episode last year that forced him to cancel a tour.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all counts in the Boston Marathon bombing trial. The author argues that understanding radicalization—not Islam itself—is key to preventing future attacks, noting that extremists exploit real grievances over global conflicts affecting Muslims. The piece contends that showing young Muslims that violence harms rather than helps their communities is more effective than debates over reforming Islam.

This week's top videos: Mike Tyson's abandoned Ohio mansion, once featuring an indoor pool and gold Jacuzzi, is set to become a church. Elsewhere, CNN examined sexual assault allegations against Bikram yoga founder Bikram Choudhury and interviewed a witness to the Germanwings crash in the French Alps. Other clips featured a debate over Indiana's religious freedom law, the world's fastest roller coaster, and a physics study on facial attractiveness.

Coalition forces have retaken 25-30% of Iraqi territory from ISIS, according to a Pentagon map, with gains concentrated in central and northern Iraq. Analyst Afzal Ashraf says the advances reflect a conventional frontal push rather than more effective "maneuverist warfare," and that ISIS is compensating for territorial losses with attacks elsewhere, such as Ramadi and Syria, to project strength and sustain recruitment.

A passenger on an Air Canada flight from Toronto to Atlanta attempted to choke Oliver Minatel, a soccer player with the Ottawa Fury Football Club, using headphone cords mid-flight. Other passengers intervened to stop the attack, and the suspect, who claimed the team was trying to kill him, was restrained until landing. The FBI confirmed the suspect was taken for a medical/mental evaluation, with no federal charges currently pending.

Rurik Jutting, a 29-year-old British former banker, is charged with murdering two women, Sumarti Ningsih and Seneng Mujiasih, whose bodies were found at his Hong Kong apartment last November. A court hearing to assess evidence before trial was adjourned until May, pending analysis of over 200 forensic and DNA samples. Both victims were Indonesian women working in Hong Kong; their bodies have since been repatriated and buried.

Tornadoes swept through the rural Midwest on Thursday, killing one person in Fairdale, Illinois, and destroying dozens of homes near Rochelle, including that of newly elected Ogle County Sheriff Brian VanVickle. Officials reported 20 homes destroyed and up to 100 damaged, though most residents escaped serious injury thanks to early warnings. Additional tornadoes touched down in Iowa and Missouri, following eight reported Wednesday in Oklahoma, Kansas and Missouri.

Don McLean's original manuscript for "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at a Christie's auction, marking the third-highest price ever paid for an American literary manuscript. McLean, nearing 70, said he decided to sell to secure his family's financial future. The 16-page draft includes unused lyrics and notes that may shed light on the song's famously debated meaning.

UNRWA Commissioner-General Pierre Krähenbühl will make an emergency visit to Syria's Yarmouk refugee camp to assess the humanitarian crisis affecting 18,000 remaining Palestinians and Syrians. The camp, largely controlled by ISIS and Al-Nusra Front, has been besieged since 2013, with reports of malnutrition and barrel bombings. Its population has fallen from 160,000 in 2011 to roughly 18,000 today.

Saudi-led coalition airstrikes have pounded Houthi-held Sanaa and other Yemeni areas for over a week, killing roughly 600 people, knocking out power for 16 million, and prompting the Red Cross to appeal for a humanitarian ceasefire. The UN Security Council discussed a Russian draft resolution calling for a halt to strikes but reached no decision, while chaos has also allowed al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula to expand its control in eastern Yemen.

Former Australia cricket captain and legendary broadcaster Richie Benaud has died at age 84, following treatment for skin cancer. Benaud captained Australia through an unbeaten 28 Tests before becoming cricket's most famous commentator, spending decades with the BBC alongside his work in Australia. Tributes poured in from Australian PM Tony Abbott, cricketers Michael Clarke and Shane Warne, and figures across the cricketing world.

A brief total lunar eclipse, lasting just 4 minutes and 43 seconds, occurred early Saturday, visible best in western North America and parts of South America, Asia and Russia. NASA called it the shortest total lunar eclipse of the century, caused by Earth's shadow engulfing the moon and often producing a reddish "blood moon" effect. It was the third in a series of four consecutive lunar eclipses, or "tetrad," with the final one set for September 28.

A federal grand jury indicted Robert Durst on a firearms charge after authorities found a .38 caliber revolver in his hotel room last month. Durst, 71, already faces a first-degree murder charge in Los Angeles for the 2000 killing of Susan Berman and awaits extradition there, while also facing weapons and drugs charges in New Orleans. His attorney says Durst suffers from serious health issues and autism.

Paul Walker died in a November 2013 car crash while on break from filming "Furious 7," which releases Friday. Producers rewrote the script and used his brothers as body doubles to complete his scenes, and the film includes a tribute to him as his character is "retired." Fans and co-stars, including Vin Diesel, have paid tribute to Walker, who is remembered for his kindness both on and off screen.

Model Manuela Arbelaez accidentally revealed the correct price for a Hyundai Sonata on "The Price Is Right," giving the contestant a free car. Host Drew Carey laughed as a mortified Arbelaez tried to hide, but she later tweeted that everything turned out fine. The gaffe capped a notable week for the show, which saw former host Bob Barker, 91, return to host on Wednesday.

Thai Smile, a Thai Airways subsidiary, unveiled an Airbus A320 decorated with "Adventure Time" characters at Bangkok's Suvarnabhumi Airport. The livery, featuring Jake, Finn and Princess Bubblegum, extends to the cabin interior and resulted from a partnership with Cartoon Network Amazone water park. The inaugural themed flight departs Bangkok for Phuket on April 4.

Pedestrians in Washington, D.C., used an umbrella to corral a mother duck and her ducklings after they crossed a busy street, halting traffic to help them cross safely. CNN journalists Brian Todd and Khalil Abdallah witnessed the scene while en route to another assignment. The ducks were eventually led to a grassy area at 16th and L streets NW.

French police have finished collecting evidence from the Germanwings Flight 9525 crash site, with a private security firm now guarding the area. Investigators found both black boxes and isolated 150 DNA profiles from over 2,000 samples, though the crash killed all 150 aboard. Authorities maintain co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately crashed the plane, having concealed a diagnosis that he was unfit for work.

Cuba attended the Summit of the Americas in Panama for the first time in over 50 years without U.S. objection, marking a diplomatic milestone amid ongoing negotiations to restore U.S.-Cuba relations. Cuban officials say full diplomatic ties depend on the U.S. removing Cuba from its terrorism sponsor list, a move the State Department has now recommended to the White House. Tensions also simmer over Cuba's alliance with Venezuela, which Washington recently deemed a national security concern, though officials have since softened that stance.

Jesus and his disciples lived at subsistence level, relying on begging, hospitality, and donations rather than steady income, according to biblical scholars. Wealthy supporters—including women like Mary Magdalene and Joanna, and men like Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus—helped fund his itinerant ministry from their own resources. This financial arrangement, hinted at throughout the Gospels, reveals the practical realities behind Jesus' teachings on poverty and wealth.

The California Public Utilities Commission has fined Pacific Gas & Electric Co. a record $1.6 billion for unsafe operation of its gas transmission system, including the 2010 San Bruno pipeline explosion that killed eight people. Most of the penalty will fund pipeline safety improvements, with PG&E's CEO saying the company is working to become the safest energy provider in the U.S. PG&E has already paid over $500 million in victim claims and replaced more than 800 miles of pipe since the disaster.

Lauren Hill, the Indiana college basketball player whose battle against brain cancer inspired people worldwide, has died at age 19. Hill, who was diagnosed with an inoperable brain tumor in 2013, fulfilled her dream of playing for Mount St. Joseph University after the NCAA moved up her team's season opener, and she helped raise $1.4 million for pediatric cancer research. Tributes poured in from figures including LeBron James and NCAA President Mark Emmert, who praised her courage and lasting legacy.

A fire broke out Friday morning at the General Electric Appliance Park in Louisville, Kentucky, sending thick smoke and flames into the air. Officials said no injuries were reported, though the blaze reached at least four alarms and its cause remains unknown.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, key negotiator in the Iran nuclear talks with US Secretary of State John Kerry, is known publicly as polished and jovial, but lesser-known facts reveal a more complex history. These include his education in the US during Iran's 1979 revolution, conflicting birth years listed by his own ministry, past investigation over an Iranian charity accused of laundering money, and his early activism seizing the Iranian consulate in San Francisco. He has now spent more face time with Kerry than any other foreign minister as they work toward a June 30 deadline.

A Connecticut judge denied a motion to let 17-year-old "Cassandra C.," who is undergoing forced chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma, return home, keeping her in state custody. Cassandra, now in remission, initially resisted treatment but her attorney says she now wants to complete it, with chemo expected to end this month. The state has said it will withdraw its neglect petition and allow her home once treatment concludes.

Researchers at the University of Texas at Austin used computer software to analyze word patterns in "Double Falsehood," a 1728 play credited to Lewis Theobald, and concluded it was largely written by Shakespeare with help from John Fletcher. The study found only minimal traces of Theobald's writing style, suggesting he edited rather than authored the work. Some scholars praised the research's objectivity, though skeptics are expected to remain unconvinced.

Marseille prosecutor Brice Robin denied reports of cockpit video footage from Germanwings Flight 9525, contradicting claims by Bild and Paris Match magazines. Separately, Lufthansa confirmed co-pilot Andreas Lubitz had disclosed a "previous episode of severe depression" to its flight school in 2009, raising questions about why he was allowed to fly. Investigators are examining whether Lubitz feared losing his pilot's license due to medical issues as a possible motive for the crash that killed all 150 aboard.

American Samoan veteran Emy Afalava, denied citizenship despite being born on U.S. soil, has filed a federal lawsuit challenging his status, with a ruling expected soon from the D.C. Circuit. The case echoes historic Supreme Court decisions—Dred Scott and Gonzalez v. Williams—that denied full citizenship rights based on race. American Samoans remain the only U.S. territory residents not granted citizenship, more than a century after annexation.

Blue Bell has shut down its Broken Arrow, Oklahoma plant after listeria contamination was found in ice cream traced to the facility, part of a widening outbreak linked to the company's products. Five people in Kansas were sickened and three died after consuming Blue Bell items at one hospital, marking the company's first recall in its 108-year history. The CDC continues investigating whether the ice cream is definitively the source of separate outbreaks in Kansas and Texas.

Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for an attack on Garissa University College in Kenya that killed many and took hostages, marking an escalation of the group's activities across East Africa. The Somalia-based group, which split from Al-Ittihad al-Islami in 2003 and later pledged allegiance to al-Qaeda, has increasingly targeted Kenya since 2011, exploiting regional instability, poverty and governance failures to fuel recruitment. Analysts argue lasting security requires addressing these root causes, not just military responses.

A Russian SU-27 intercepted a U.S. RC-135U reconnaissance plane over the Baltic Sea in what the Pentagon called an "unsafe and unprofessional" maneuver, prompting a formal diplomatic complaint to Moscow. Russia disputed the account, claiming the U.S. plane had its transponder off, a claim U.S. officials denied. A similar incident occurred a year earlier over the Sea of Okhotsk.

Artist Phillip Hyman created a hooded, black-winged angel artwork from reclaimed wood to mourn Walter Scott, an unarmed black man shot by a North Charleston police officer. The piece, symbolizing Scott ascending to heaven, has become an icon of the Black Lives Matter movement, with protesters using it at rallies outside City Hall. Hyman said the art reflects broader issues of police violence across America, from Ferguson to Florida.

Officer Michael Slager was fired and charged with murder after cellphone video showed him shooting Walter Scott, an unarmed black man, as he ran away in North Charleston. The footage contradicts Slager's account that Scott had grabbed his Taser, and police reports from officers at the scene also show discrepancies over whether CPR was administered to Scott. The South Carolina Law Enforcement Division is investigating.

ISIS claimed its fighters stormed Iraq's Baiji oil refinery and seized several buildings, though Iraqi officials denied the claim and insisted government forces retain full control. The refinery, a strategic resource near recently recaptured Tikrit, has been fought over before, and damage could significantly impact Iraq's domestic fuel supply.

Nashville's district attorney banned prosecutors from offering female sterilization in plea deals, sparking outrage, though the practice—and male sterilization/castration in plea deals—has occurred nationwide for years. The Supreme Court has never fully addressed whether sterilization as punishment is constitutional, but voluntary waiver in plea deals likely makes it permissible. The author argues public outrage stems largely from gender bias, since sterilizing men has drawn far less scrutiny than sterilizing women.

The Ebola epidemic has infected over 25,000 people and killed more than 10,000, though new weekly cases have dropped to their lowest level since May 2014. While Liberia and Sierra Leone have seen cases decline sharply, Guinea still reports unsafe burials and post-mortem diagnoses, raising concerns about undetected transmission chains.

The NCAA is arguing in court that it bears no legal responsibility for ensuring athletes actually receive an education, contradicting its public messaging about academics being paramount. The claim comes in response to a lawsuit from former UNC athletes over the school's academic fraud scandal, and critics say it mirrors the NCAA's similar denial of responsibility for athlete health and safety in other lawsuits. Critics argue this undermines the NCAA's stated mission and raises questions about its purpose and tax-exempt status.

An explosion and fire at a paraxylene chemical plant in Zhangzhou, Fujian province, injured six people after an oil leak, Chinese state media reported. More than 600 firefighters brought the blaze under control; no toxic chemical spill was reported. The plant, previously relocated from Xiamen after 2007 protests over pollution concerns, also suffered an explosion in 2013.

A bystander's video showing Officer Michael Slager shooting Walter Scott in the back as he fled contradicts the officer's self-defense claims and exposes alleged evidence tampering. The author argues that police body cameras could have prevented the shooting and would help address the broader crisis of racial bias and eroding trust between police and minority communities. While cameras are only an interim fix, tackling systemic bias requires tougher hiring standards, better training, and long-term social change.

The Summit of the Americas, expected to focus on a historic US-Cuba rapprochement, has instead become tense amid clashes with Venezuela. President Maduro has accused the US of plotting a coup and rallied regional allies, including Cuba, against Washington's sanctions on Venezuelan officials. The dispute risks overshadowing the anticipated Obama-Castro meeting in Panama City.

A fire broke out on a Russian nuclear submarine undergoing repairs in a dry dock at the Zvyozdochka shipyard, reportedly ignited by welding work on rubber insulation. Officials said the vessel had no nuclear fuel, weapons or hazardous materials aboard, and no injuries were reported.

Tropical storm Maysak, downgraded from super typhoon status, approached the Philippines Saturday with winds exceeding 70 mph. Authorities evacuated residents, banned tourists from coastal areas, and restricted water activities as officials warned of flash floods and landslides. The storm was expected to make landfall in Isabela province Sunday before exiting the Philippines by Monday.

Deion Sanders publicly mocked his son Deion Sanders Jr. on Twitter after the SMU wide receiver claimed he only eats "hood doughnuts." The NFL legend reminded his 912,000 followers that his son has a trust fund, a condo and his own clothing line, telling him to "stop the hood stuff." Sanders Jr. took the roasting in stride, retweeting his father's comments.

Guatemala has one of the world's highest femicide rates, with two women killed daily amid a culture of impunity rooted in the country's civil war and entrenched machismo. Survivor Adelma Cifuentes, who lost an arm in an attempted murder by her abusive husband, now uses theater to help other women, while government reforms, NGOs, and community programs offer some hope for change. Despite these efforts, weak law enforcement and deep-seated discrimination leave millions of women vulnerable.

Police in Malegaon, India, are requiring residents to photograph their cattle and submit "mugshots" with identifying details to help enforce a new state ban on beef sale and consumption. The Maharashtra law, prompted by a recent cow slaughter case, criminalizes killing bulls and bullocks and imposes up to five years in prison for beef consumption or sale, sparking a beef traders' strike and legal challenges. Other Indian states, including Haryana, have similarly tightened cow slaughter laws, with national officials considering a countrywide ban.

Lucknow police in India have purchased pepper-spray-equipped drones to control violent protests and mobs, at a cost of $9,560 to $19,300 each. Critics warn the move could suppress free speech and reflects an authoritarian approach rather than dialogue-based solutions. The drones, also used for crowd monitoring at festivals, are set to be officially launched by Uttar Pradesh's Chief Minister later this month.

Don McLean's handwritten manuscript for "American Pie," his 1971 anthem inspired by the 1959 plane crash that killed Buddy Holly, sold at Christie's for $1.2 million to an unnamed buyer. The song, ranked by the Recording Industry of America and National Endowment of the Arts as the fifth greatest of the 20th century, remains an enduring cultural touchstone 44 years after its release.

A gang burglarized a Hatton Garden vault in London's jewelry district over the Easter weekend, evoking comparisons to heist films and the 1971 Baker Street bank robbery. Former Scotland Yard commander Roy Ramm explains that such sophisticated crimes require meticulous planning, trusted criminal networks, and often inside information, with cash and easily convertible valuables like gold and jewelry being preferred targets. Police will now pursue forensic evidence, CCTV footage, and criminal intelligence networks to identify the perpetrators.

7-Eleven is holding its first Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day on Saturday, letting customers fill any container up to 10 inches in diameter for $1.49. The promotion, distinct from the annual Free Slurpee Day on July 11, kicks off peak Slurpee season.

Georgia Davis Powers, Kentucky's first Black state senator, criticizes Rand Paul's presidential campaign launch, arguing his outreach message to minority voters is undermined by his record on civil rights, voting rights, and social issues. She contends Paul's positions—including past comments on the Civil Rights Act and opposition to a stronger Voting Rights Act—are outdated and disqualifying. Powers concludes that Americans deserve better than Paul's candidacy.

A Lamborghini crashed into a guardrail Sunday at the Exotic Driving Experience at Walt Disney World Speedway, killing passenger Gary Terry, 36. Driver Tavon Watson, 24, lost control of the vehicle and suffered minor injuries. Petty Holdings, which operates the attraction, expressed condolences over the crash.

Aaron Hernandez's defense rested Monday after less than a day of testimony in his murder trial for the 2013 killing of Odin Lloyd, following months of prosecution witnesses. Key disputes include Hernandez's contradictory statements to Patriots owner Robert Kraft, his fiancee's testimony about disposing of a box, footwear impression analysis, and whether he was holding a gun or an iPad in home security footage. Closing arguments are set for Tuesday, with Hernandez still facing a separate double-murder trial after this case concludes.

Chinese authorities detained feminist activist Wu Rongrong and four colleagues after they planned an International Women's Day protest against sexual harassment, charging them with "creating disturbances." Their case must be resolved by April 13, when they will either be released or formally arrested, a step that typically leads to conviction in China's legal system. The crackdown comes despite Beijing's push for an anti-domestic violence law and the 20th anniversary of the Fourth World Conference on Women.

Martin O'Malley told Iowa reporters that Hillary Clinton's frontrunner status is not guaranteed, citing her 2008 loss to Obama as precedent. Despite polling at just 1% nationally and in Iowa, O'Malley continued teasing a presidential run, saying Democrats deserve a "robust conversation" rather than an uncontested primary. Clinton is expected to formally launch her campaign Sunday via a social media video.

Aaron Hernandez was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison for killing Odin Lloyd in June 2013. At the sentencing, Lloyd's mother, sister and uncle gave emotional testimony describing him as a devoted family man, before his mother said she forgave those responsible for his death.

Ted Cruz campaigned across Iowa last week, emphasizing his Christian faith and religious liberty to court the state's influential evangelical voter base ahead of the 2016 caucuses. As the only declared GOP presidential candidate, he drew large crowds and defended Indiana's religious freedom law amid national controversy. Cruz aims to combine evangelical support with tea party and libertarian voters, though rivals like Huckabee, Santorum and others are also vying for the same religious conservative bloc.

Marvel and other studios released a flurry of superhero images and casting news within 24 hours, including a poster of Paul Bettany as the Vision in "Avengers: Age of Ultron" and a look at Charlie Cox's Daredevil suit ahead of the Netflix series premiere. Additional reveals included Ben Hardy as Angel in "X-Men: Apocalypse" and Jamie Bell's CGI version of The Thing in the rebooted "Fantastic Four."

The Italian Coast Guard rescued 978 migrants in the Mediterranean Sea on Friday, off the coast of Libya. More than 10,000 migrants, mostly from West Africa, Somalia and Syria, arrived in Italy in the first quarter of 2015, with at least 480 dying en route, up sharply from fewer than 50 deaths during the same period last year.

French network TV5Monde regained control of one of its 11 channels and its Facebook page Thursday, a day after a "extremely powerful cyberattack" knocked out its broadcasts, social media accounts and websites. A group claiming ISIS affiliation took credit via hacked social media posts, though no formal claim of responsibility was made. The network reaches 260 million homes worldwide under a partnership between France, Canada, Switzerland and Belgium's Wallonia-Brussels Federation.

David Lynch announced he will not direct the "Twin Peaks" revival, citing insufficient funding from Showtime to produce it properly. Showtime expressed sadness over the decision, saying it still hopes to bring back the series with both creators, Lynch and Mark Frost. Actor Kyle MacLachlan had previously confirmed he would reprise his role as FBI agent Dale Cooper.

Massachusetts hosted closing arguments in two high-profile trials: the Boston Marathon bombing case against Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, whose jury began deliberations, and the murder trial of former NFL player Aaron Hernandez. Meanwhile, Sen. Rand Paul officially launched his presidential campaign, Chicago voters headed to a runoff between Mayor Rahm Emanuel and challenger Jesus "Chuy" Garcia, and Ferguson, Missouri held municipal elections shaped by the fallout from Michael Brown's shooting.

Multiple tornadoes were reported across Kansas and Missouri Wednesday night, with sightings near Goddard and Aetna, Kansas, and a possible touchdown in Potosi, Missouri, which suffered wind damage and flooding. Nighttime tornadoes pose heightened danger, CNN's Chad Myers warned, as more storms hit the Midwest and southern Great Lakes region Thursday.

Jodi Arias was sentenced to life in prison without parole for the 2008 murder of ex-boyfriend Travis Alexander, after two juries deadlocked on the death penalty. Arias expressed remorse before sentencing, while Alexander's sisters gave emotional victim impact statements. She will serve her sentence at Arizona State Prison Complex-Perryville.

The EPA found traces of methyl bromide, a restricted pesticide banned for indoor use, at a Delaware family's rented villa in St. John's Sirenusa resort after they fell seriously ill in March. The illness followed a March 18 fumigation by Terminix, which was hired for pest control at a nearby unit, and the Justice Department has launched a criminal investigation. The EPA continues testing to determine how the exposure occurred and prevent future incidents.

A Columbia Journalism School review found systemic editorial failures behind Rolling Stone's discredited UVA gang rape story, prompting an apology from managing editor Will Dana. Legal experts say UVA, as a public institution, cannot sue for defamation, but Phi Kappa Psi fraternity members might succeed if they can prove the "small group" exception applies and demonstrate tangible damages.

FBI agents shot and wounded armed robbery suspect Kevone Charleston, 36, during an attempted takedown at a Forsyth County, Georgia, CVS on Saturday. Charleston, suspected in 32 commercial robberies since 2013, rammed several FBI vehicles while fleeing, injuring two agents who were treated and released. Charleston's injuries are not life-threatening, and he is now in custody.

Alaska Airlines Flight 448 made an emergency landing back at Seattle-Tacoma after passengers heard banging and screams from the cargo hold. A Menzies Aviation ramp agent had fallen asleep inside; he was unharmed, passed a drug test, and was released from the hospital. The plane later continued to Los Angeles as the airline investigates.

A North Carolina judge ruled Monday that Craig Hicks' case is "death penalty qualified" in the killings of three Muslim college students in Chapel Hill. Hicks, 46, is charged with first-degree murder in the February shooting deaths of his neighbors Yusor Mohammad, Deah Shaddy Barakat and Razan Mohammad Abu-Salha. Authorities have cited a parking dispute as a possible factor but have not ruled out investigating the case as a hate crime.

Amnesty International's report "Their Lives on the Line" highlights escalating attacks on women's rights activists in Afghanistan by the Taliban, warlords, and government officials, noting perpetrators are rarely held accountable. The report follows the brutal mob killing of Farkhunda in Kabul, whose funeral saw women act as pallbearers for the first time, symbolizing defiance. Activists like Selay Ghaffer vow to continue the struggle despite personal threats, calling it the start of an uprising against violence and patriarchy.

A New York judge has authorized serving divorce papers to a husband via Facebook private message, highlighting the evolving law of "service of process." The article explains traditional alternate methods—like nailing papers to a door or publishing notices in obscure journals—are often unreliable, making electronic service a practical, if novel, solution. The author argues online service is a logical progression, since most people are more reliably reachable online than at a fixed address.

Rev. Robert H. Schuller, founder of the "Hour of Power" television ministry and Crystal Cathedral megachurch, died Thursday at age 88 after battling esophageal cancer. Schuller rose from humble Iowa roots to build a televangelism empire preaching "possibility thinking," but his later years were marked by a family succession dispute and the 2010 bankruptcy of Crystal Cathedral Ministries.

Four workers were killed and 45 injured when a fire broke out on Pemex's Abkatun Permanente oil platform in the Gulf of Mexico's Campeche Sound. About 300 people were evacuated and more than 10 boats battled the blaze, which was extinguished by Wednesday night. Pemex denied reports the platform collapsed and said no oil spill occurred; the cause remains unknown.

Kansas Gov. Sam Brownback signed a first-of-its-kind law banning the dilation and evacuation abortion procedure, commonly used in second-trimester abortions, except to protect the mother's life or health. Supporters called it a landmark step in restricting abortion, while Planned Parenthood and other critics warned it endangers women and represents the nation's most restrictive abortion law. Both sides expect further legislative and legal battles over similar measures in other states.

CCTV host Bi Fujian sparked controversy after a leaked video showed him cursing Chairman Mao Zedong at a private dinner party. Bi apologized publicly on Weibo, while CCTV said it would investigate the incident, which has divided opinion online. Mao remains a polarizing figure in China, revered by some but blamed by others for mass suffering during his rule.

Kentucky guard Andrew Harrison apologized for a hot-mic slur directed at Wisconsin's Frank Kaminsky after Saturday's Final Four loss. Harrison said the comment was made "in jest" and called Kaminsky to apologize, who said he was "over it." Harrison wished Kaminsky luck in Monday's championship game against Duke.

"Arrested Development" executive producer Brian Grazer revealed on a podcast that the show will return for a fifth season of 17 episodes. Netflix, which streamed the fourth season exclusively in 2013 after Fox's cancellation, declined to confirm the news. It remains unclear whether the full cast will return.

CERN's Large Hadron Collider has restarted after a two-year shutdown, with beams circulating again inside its 17-mile ring. The $3.3 billion machine aims to recreate conditions after the Big Bang, helping scientists probe dark matter, antimatter and gaps in the Standard Model of physics. Officials say the next key step is ramping up beam energy to record levels.

An Iranian observation aircraft flew within 50 yards of a U.S. Navy helicopter over the Persian Gulf this month, prompting concern among American officials that the maneuver could have escalated into a serious incident. U.S. officials believe the move may have been locally ordered rather than sanctioned by top Iranian commanders, noting the aircraft was not seen again for two weeks afterward. No shots were fired, and Washington is considering a formal protest against Tehran.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all 30 counts, including 17 capital charges, in the Boston Marathon bombing trial after roughly 11½ hours of jury deliberation. The trial now moves to a penalty phase, where jurors will decide whether the 21-year-old should be sentenced to death. His defense, led by attorney Judy Clarke, had focused on portraying his late older brother as the plot's mastermind in hopes of sparing his life.

Indian police arrested four employees of ethnic-wear chain FabIndia after a federal minister discovered a security camera overlooking a changing room at a Goa store. The store's manager remains at large, and authorities have sealed the outlet while FabIndia cooperates with the investigation. Those arrested face voyeurism and privacy breach charges, carrying up to three years in jail.

Iran will lift its ban on women attending some men's sports events, with the change for indoor sports expected within the next year, a deputy sports minister said. The ban, imposed after the 1979 Islamic Revolution, has drawn international pressure, including criticism from FIFA President Sepp Blatter over its exclusion from soccer stadiums.

Ramalinga Raju, founder of Satyam Computers Services, and nine others were sentenced to seven years in jail for their roles in India's biggest corporate fraud scandal. Raju admitted in 2009 to inflating profits by $1.6 billion using fictitious assets and cash, prompting comparisons to the Enron scandal. Satyam was later sold to Tech Mahindra after the Indian government dismissed its board.

Alaska Airlines removed cancer patient Elizabeth Sedway and her family from a Hawaii-to-San Jose flight after she mentioned feeling weak, citing lack of a doctor's note despite no prior requirement. The airline later apologized, refunded the family's tickets, and covered their overnight accommodations, though Sedway said the delay caused her to miss chemotherapy and disrupted her family's schedule.

Turkish singer-songwriter Kayahan died of cancer Friday in Istanbul at age 66, five days after his birthday. First diagnosed with cancer in 1990, he had battled the disease intermittently for over two decades while continuing to perform, most recently on Valentine's Day. Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu praised his contributions to Turkish music, which included nearly 20 albums and numerous beloved love songs.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu criticized the Iran nuclear deal on CNN, arguing for continued pressure rather than accepting "this bad deal or war," while insisting his opposition isn't rooted in personal animosity toward Obama. Democrats like Sen. Dianne Feinstein urged Netanyahu to tone down his rhetoric, while Republicans like Sen. Lindsey Graham argued for maintaining sanctions until a new president negotiates a better agreement. Energy Secretary Ernest Moniz defended the framework, saying it would extend Iran's nuclear "breakout" time and block pathways to a bomb.

A domestic kidnapping in Washington led to two shootings Thursday night, police said. A Census Bureau security guard was shot and critically wounded after approaching a suspect's vehicle in Suitland, Maryland, and the suspect then fled, leading police on a chase that ended in a crash and shootout on Washington's H Street. An officer and the suspect were wounded, and the kidnapping victim was found safe.

Chelsea Manning, serving a 35-year sentence for leaking classified documents, has joined Twitter by dictating tweets via phone to a communications firm, since she lacks internet access in prison. Manning, who has been undergoing hormone therapy for gender dysphoria, already has more than 26,000 followers. She was convicted in 2013 for disseminating 750,000 documents to WikiLeaks.

Rapper Nelly was arrested on drug charges in Putnam County, Tennessee, after a trooper stopped his tour bus for missing DOT stickers and smelled marijuana. A search uncovered methamphetamine, marijuana, drug paraphernalia and several firearms. Nelly posted bond and was released from jail.

A Delaware family fell critically ill after suspected methyl bromide pesticide exposure at a rented villa in St. John, U.S. Virgin Islands; the father is now stable while his two sons remain in critical condition. The EPA found the toxic pesticide, restricted for indoor use, present in the unit, and the rental agent has since terminated its contract with pest control company Terminix. The Justice Department has launched a criminal investigation into the incident.

Online bloggers and journalists across Asia face growing legal persecution and violence as authoritarian governments crack down on dissent, with Singapore, Malaysia, China and Vietnam jailing critics under various charges. In Bangladesh, the danger has turned deadly, with two bloggers hacked to death in the past five weeks for writing critically about Islam, part of a pattern of killings carried out with near-total impunity. CPJ data shows online journalists are increasingly targeted worldwide, as they operate outside the protections and constraints of mainstream media.

Nina Dobrev announced she is leaving "The Vampire Diaries" after six seasons, sparking backlash from fans upset over her exit and the show's planned seventh season without her. Producer Julie Plec expressed support for Dobrev's decision, while Dobrev urged fans to watch the remaining episodes leading to May's season finale.

Syria's Yarmouk refugee camp, once home to over 100,000 Palestinians, has been devastated by years of civil war, worsened by an ISIS raid two weeks ago and subsequent government bombing. Only about 18,000 residents remain amid severe shortages of food, water and medicine, with aid groups largely unable to reach them. Despite the destruction, many residents refuse to abandon their homes.

NASA scientists estimate roughly 40 billion Earth-like habitable-zone planets exist in the Milky Way, making primitive life elsewhere likely. However, intelligent, communicative civilizations are far rarer and harder to detect, given the tiny window in which humans have used radio technology. Upcoming missions, including the James Webb Space Telescope, will search for biological signatures on exoplanets, but contact with advanced alien life remains highly improbable in the near term.

Massachusetts man Carlos Colina, 32, faces murder charges after human remains found in a duffel bag and an apartment building in Cambridge were identified as Jonathan Camilien, 26. Police discovered the remains Saturday after a tip about a suspicious item, then traced surveillance footage to find more body parts nearby. Colina, who knew the victim, was already facing separate assault charges before the murder charge was filed.

Kanye West settled a civil lawsuit with paparazzi photographer Daniel Ramos, whom he had assaulted at LAX in 2013, with the two shaking hands after West issued an apology. West previously pleaded no contest to misdemeanor battery in the case, receiving probation, anger management and community service. Ramos' attorney Gloria Allred said the case affirmed that celebrities are not above the law.

Critics argue Obama's political stake in securing an Iran nuclear legacy has weakened America's negotiating position, resulting in a framework deal that lets Iran keep significant nuclear infrastructure and enrichment capacity. The agreement, announced after a missed deadline, falls far short of Obama's earlier pledge to end Iran's nuclear program entirely, alarming regional allies like Saudi Arabia. Sanctions relief will begin quickly while Iran retains a "breakout" capability, prompting fears of regional instability and proliferation.

A bystander video showing officer Michael Slager fatally shooting Walter Scott has led to murder charges and renewed scrutiny of police killings nationwide. The piece notes a 1994 federal law requiring the Justice Department to collect data on police use of excessive force has never been properly enforced, leaving comprehensive nationwide statistics unavailable. The author calls for stronger federal action to mandate such data collection, citing gaps filled only by media investigations and independent trackers.

Five Americans exposed to Ebola in Sierra Leone have been released from an Omaha hospital after three weeks of monitoring, none having developed the virus. The Partners in Health clinicians had contact with a colleague who contracted Ebola and remains in fair condition at the NIH. The West African epidemic has killed more than 10,000 people since December 2013.

Mark Ronson's "Uptown Funk!" featuring Bruno Mars logged its 13th week atop the Billboard Hot 100, making it the decade's longest-leading No. 1 and putting it among just 10 songs ever to hold the top spot for 13-plus weeks. Elsewhere in the top 10, Natalie La Rose's debut single "Somebody," featuring Jeremih, cracked the top 10 for the first time, while The Weeknd's "Earned It" rose to No. 5 and topped the R&B/Hip-Hop chart.

Twitter marked "Rex Manning Day" from the 1995 film "Empire Records" on April 8, coinciding with "Lost" fans' own date celebration. The article highlights other notable movie dates, including "Titanic's" April 14, "Miss Congeniality's" April 25, "Mean Girls Day" on October 3, and "Back to the Future Part II's" October 21, 2015.

"Grace of Monaco," the Nicole Kidman-led biopic that opened last year's Cannes Film Festival, will bypass U.S. theaters and premiere on Lifetime May 25, following poor international box office and a public feud between director Olivier Dahan and Weinstein Co. chief Harvey Weinstein over the final cut. The film, which drew criticism from Grace Kelly's own children for being "historically inaccurate," also stars Tim Roth, Frank Langella and Parker Posey.

Tokyo's Shibuya ward passed an ordinance allowing same-sex couples to receive "partnership certificates," granting limited rights such as hospital visitation and joint tenancy agreements, though the measure is not legally binding. Activists hailed the move as a significant step toward marriage equality in Japan, though achieving full equal rights would require national legislation. Neighboring Setagaya ward is considering similar measures, while conservative groups have criticized the decision.

California's fourth-year drought, which prompted Gov. Jerry Brown to order a mandatory 25% urban water cutback, is driving up US grocery prices since the state grows a third of the nation's vegetables and two-thirds of its fruits and nuts. Berries, grapes, broccoli and other produce rose in price last year, while a separate Texas-Oklahoma drought pushed beef prices up 12.1%; experts remain uncertain whether this year's impact will be as severe. Tourists visiting California will notice new water-saving measures like restaurants withholding water unless requested, though wine grape harvests have remained excellent despite the drought.

The University of Michigan reversed a decision to cancel a campus screening of "American Sniper" after backlash to its initial cancellation, which followed a student petition citing negative portrayals of Middle Easterners. University officials called the cancellation a mistake inconsistent with free expression values. An alternative screening of "Paddington" will be offered for those who prefer not to attend.

Amy Schumer hosted the 2015 MTV Movie Awards, delivering a hit opening segment and monologue, though a bow-and-arrow gag misfired literally. Highlights included Channing Tatum twerking for Jennifer Lopez, Rebel Wilson's slip-up introducing "Pitch Perfect 2," and Robert Downey Jr.'s Avengers castmates kneeling as he accepted the Generation Award. Weaker moments included Shailene Woodley's rambling speech and a recycled Zac Efron-Dave Franco gag.

A fiberglass boat fragment believed to be debris from Japan's 2011 tsunami was found off Oregon's coast and towed to Newport this week. Biologists discovered live yellowtail jack fish, native to Japanese waters, inside the wreckage. The boat will be destroyed, while the fish will go to the Oregon Coast Aquarium.

A year after Boko Haram abducted nearly 300 schoolgirls from Chibok, Nigeria, most remain missing, with fears they have been raped, enslaved or forced to convert. President-elect Muhammadu Buhari marked the anniversary by pledging to fight the militant group, which still controls parts of northeastern Nigeria. The hashtag #BringBackOurGirls continues to trend worldwide as families await news of their daughters.

An op-ed explains the Christian "Easter Triduum" — Good Friday, Holy Saturday and Easter Sunday — tracing the progression from Jesus's crucifixion through a period of anxious suspension to resurrection. The author argues this cycle of suffering, waiting and renewal mirrors patterns humans repeatedly experience in everyday life, not just on the religious calendar. Unlike Christmas, the piece contends, Easter's deeper meaning resists commercialization and secular co-option.

Kenya froze 86 bank accounts linked to suspected Al-Shabaab supporters following last week's massacre of 147 people at Garissa University College. Mourners gathered in Nairobi to honor victims as questions mounted over delayed police response despite prior intelligence warnings. Kenya also launched airstrikes on Al-Shabaab camps in Somalia and offered a $215,000 reward for the attack's alleged organizer.

Jia Jiang quit his job to become an entrepreneur, then launched a "100 Days of Rejection" blog after his startup was denied funding, seeking out rejection through bizarre requests like asking a Krispy Kreme manager to make Olympic-symbol donuts. The project went viral, leading to his new book "Rejection Proof," which teaches readers to overcome fear of rejection and turn it into opportunity.

Attorney General Eric Holder issued a memo prohibiting all Justice Department personnel from soliciting prostitutes, even where legal, warning violators face suspension or firing. The directive follows a report revealing DEA agents attended cartel-funded sex parties abroad and a 2012 Secret Service scandal in Colombia.

Kenneth Morgan Stancil III has been charged in the fatal shooting of Ron Lane, a print shop operator at Wayne Community College in Goldsboro, North Carolina. Authorities are investigating whether the killing was a hate crime, noting Lane was gay and Stancil has facial tattoos possibly linked to a white supremacist gang. Stancil was arrested sleeping on a Florida beach, about 550 miles from the crime scene, after fleeing on a motorcycle.

Amnesty International's annual report reveals a troubling trend of governments using the death penalty to address terrorism and crime, with countries like Pakistan, Jordan, and Indonesia resuming or expanding executions in 2014. Despite this, global executions dropped from 778 to 607 (excluding China), and 140 states have now abolished the death penalty in law or practice. The report argues there is no evidence executions deter crime more effectively than imprisonment.

A Duke University student admitted to hanging a noose from a tree near a student union, prompting campus protests and a forum with hundreds attending. The student, unidentified due to privacy laws, has left campus and faces student conduct review, with criminal investigations ongoing. The incident follows other recent racist events at U.S. universities, including at Oklahoma and Mississippi.

Richard Dysart, the Emmy-winning actor best known for playing senior partner Leland McKenzie on NBC's "L.A. Law," has died at 86 at his Santa Monica home after a long illness. His prolific career spanned Broadway, film and television, including memorable roles in "The Hospital," "Being There," "Wall Street" and "Pale Rider." Dysart won an Emmy in 1992 for his "L.A. Law" role after four consecutive nominations, and was one of the few cast members to appear in every episode during the show's eight-season run.

Easter combines Christian religious observance—marking Christ's crucifixion and resurrection—with folk traditions like eggs and bunnies that likely originated in German culture. Its date, tied to Passover and lunar cycles, varies annually and differs between Western and Orthodox churches, which use different calendars. Pope Francis marked Holy Week at the Vatican with rain-soaked services and calls for peace amid global conflicts, while Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulcher hosted separate celebrations for Catholics, Armenians, and Eastern Orthodox Christians.

Comedian Chris Rock tweeted about being pulled over by police for the third time in seven weeks, reigniting debate over racial profiling in traffic stops. Actor Isaiah Washington sparked backlash after suggesting Rock "adapt" by driving less flashy cars, a comment he defended as meant to spark conversation. The incident follows heightened national scrutiny of police treatment of black Americans after the deaths of Eric Garner and Michael Brown.

Robert Lewis Burns Jr., original drummer for Lynyrd Skynyrd, died Friday night in a car crash near Cartersville, Georgia, after his car struck a mailbox and tree. He was 64 and not wearing a seatbelt. Burns left the band in 1975 before its lineup was later devastated by a 1977 plane crash.

A photo of a cat on stairs has gone viral, sparking online debate over whether the animal is climbing up or down. The image, posted on Imgur and amplified by 9gag.com, has drawn comparisons to the "#TheDress" optical illusion phenomenon. Advertisers have already begun capitalizing on the debate's popularity.

The US and P5+1 partners reached a framework nuclear agreement with Iran in Lausanne, limiting its nuclear program through reduced uranium stockpiles, fewer centrifuges, and rigorous inspections. The author rebuts several criticisms of the deal, including claims about its objectives, sunset clauses, and treaty status, arguing these are based on dubious assumptions rather than facts.

Rolling Stone retracted its article on an alleged UVA gang rape after a Columbia Journalism School review found major reporting failures, including not contacting Jackie's friends who disputed her account. Despite the discredited story, the underlying issue of UVA's handling of sexual assault remains under investigation by the state attorney general and the U.S. Department of Education, with the university admitting it has never expelled a student for sexual assault. Survivors and advocates worry the retraction could discourage future victims from coming forward, even as officials note legitimate concerns about UVA's practices remain unresolved.

Pacers forward Chris Copeland was stabbed early Wednesday near a New York nightclub, along with his companion Katrine Saltara and another woman, after a dispute with a 22-year-old suspect who was later arrested. Atlanta Hawks players Pero Antic and Thabo Sefolosha, who rushed to check on Copeland, were arrested on obstruction and disorderly conduct charges but were not involved in the stabbing itself. Copeland is in stable condition; both players deny wrongdoing and plan to contest the charges.

Twisted Sister announced its 2016 tour, titled "Forty and F*ck It," will be its last, marking the band's 40th anniversary. New drummer Mike Portnoy of Adrenaline Mob will replace A.J. Pero, who died in March. The band will play two tribute shows for Pero, including one benefiting his family.

John Travolta says he has not seen and does not plan to watch HBO's critical Scientology documentary "Going Clear," calling his 40-year experience with the church positive. Premiering his film "The Forger," Travolta suggested the documentary reflects "disgruntled" former members and credited Scientology with helping him survive his son Jett's 2009 death.

"Furious 7" earned a record $146 million over the weekend, with many moviegoers reporting they were emotionally moved by the film's tribute to actor Paul Walker, who died before filming was completed. The movie's producers used body doubles, CGI and Walker's brothers to finish his scenes, ultimately choosing to retire his character rather than kill him off, culminating in a montage set to the song "See You Again." Fans flooded social media with praise for the tribute, with many describing being brought to tears by the film's ending.

"Game of Thrones" returns for its fifth season Sunday, premiering simultaneously in 170 countries for the first time. Expect major story arcs to converge, including Stannis's quest for the Iron Throne intersecting with the Night's Watch, and Tyrion's path crossing with Daenerys'. The season, which surpasses George Martin's book material, will also spotlight the Stark daughters and Cersei, plus growing unrest among Westeros' common people.

Several recent survival stories highlight remarkable ocean rescues, including Louis Jordan, found after weeks adrift off North Carolina, and Jose Salvador Alvarenga, who survived over a year in the Pacific after his companion died. Other cases include fisherman Ron Ingraham rescued after 12 days near Hawaii, teenager Adrian Vasquez found after 26 days with his two companions dead, and Hiromitsu Shinkawa, rescued clinging to debris miles offshore after Japan's 2011 tsunami. Each survivor relied on ingenuity, rationed resources, and luck to endure their ordeals.

The first six "Star Wars" films will be available for digital HD download for the first time starting Friday. The collection includes bonus features offering behind-the-scenes looks at the saga, including how sound designer Ben Burtt created alien sound effects using animal recordings.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all 30 counts related to the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing, which killed several people and injured hundreds. Survivors and victims' families expressed a mix of relief, gratitude and lingering grief, with many saying the verdict brings accountability but not full closure. The sentencing phase, including whether Tsarnaev receives the death penalty, is yet to come.

China formally charged former security chief Zhou Yongkang with bribery, abuse of power and leaking state secrets, making him the highest-ranking Communist Party official ever prosecuted for corruption. Zhou, 72, once controlled China's police, spy agencies and courts before his 2012 retirement; his trial will be held in Tianjin. Analysts view his downfall as a landmark moment under President Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign, linking Zhou's case to that of disgraced leader Bo Xilai.

A Philadelphia mother has been charged after allegedly abandoning her quadriplegic, cerebral palsy-afflicted 21-year-old son in a wooded park for four days while she visited her boyfriend in Maryland. The man, found suffering from dehydration, malnutrition and other injuries, was hospitalized; police say relatives had been willing to care for him. The mother, arrested in Maryland, faces charges including aggravated assault, kidnapping and neglect, and awaits extradition to Philadelphia.

Walmart and other major corporations pressured Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson to reject a religious freedom bill, prompting him to demand changes before signing. The backlash, also seen against Indiana's similar law, highlights growing corporate support for LGBT rights and puts pressure on Republicans to reconsider their positions. GOP presidential hopefuls remain split, with Jeb Bush softening his stance while Ted Cruz criticized businesses for opposing the legislation.

A lapsed Catholic writer describes how being turned away from a priest after her brother's death drove her from the church, but Pope Francis's humility and non-judgmental tone have reawakened her faith. An interview with newly appointed Cardinal Gerald Lacroix, who emphasized the church's openness toward sinners and gay Catholics, reinforced her decision to return to Mass.

Mary Kay Letourneau Fualaau, who served over seven years in prison for raping her 13-year-old student, will mark her 10th wedding anniversary with him this month. The couple discussed their marriage, now with two teenage daughters, in an exclusive interview with ABC's "20/20." Letourneau Fualaau, now 53, also revealed plans to return to teaching and seek removal of her sex offender status.

Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign announcement has made her an unfair proxy for assessing gender equality in America, a burden no male candidate faces. The author argues this is flawed since Clinton's extensive public record, not her gender, shapes voter perceptions, and presidential races are decided primarily by partisanship and economic conditions rather than sex. Regardless of the outcome, the piece contends, drawing broad conclusions about women's political viability from Clinton's individual campaign is misguided.

Amnesty International's annual report says global executions fell 22% in 2014 to at least 607, even as death sentences rose 28% to 2,466, partly due to mass sentencing in Egypt and Nigeria. The group warns that governments, including Pakistan and China, are increasingly using the death penalty to combat real or perceived terrorism threats. Iran, Iraq, Saudi Arabia and the U.S. remained the top executioners outside China, which keeps its execution data secret.

Japan's Defense Minister Gen Nakatani told parliament that the Air Self Defense Force has never encountered an extraterrestrial UFO, responding to a question from wrestler-turned-lawmaker Antonio Inoki. Inoki, known for his political stunts and diplomatic efforts abroad, had asked whether jets are scrambled against alien threats. It marks the second time Japanese officials have publicly addressed UFO-related defense questions, following similar remarks in 2007.

Mark Wahlberg will star in "Patriots' Day," a CBS Films production about the Boston Marathon bombing and subsequent manhunt, Deadline reported. Wahlberg hopes to portray retired Boston Police Commissioner Ed Davis, with the film told from his perspective. It marks the second announced film on the bombing, following Fox's "Boston Strong."

Martin O'Malley and Jim Webb, both weighing 2016 presidential bids, appeared at a Democratic dinner in Des Moines, Iowa, showcasing contrasting styles—O'Malley eagerly worked the room while Webb remained reserved. Both trail Hillary Clinton badly in polls, with each registering around 1-3% support among Democrats. The two later pursued different paths, with O'Malley departing for New York while Webb continued campaigning in Iowa, including at a veterans' event where he seemed more comfortable.

Turkish authorities arrested nine British citizens, including four children, near the Turkey-Syria border on suspicion of trying to illegally cross into Syria. The reason for the attempted crossing was not disclosed, though Syria's ongoing conflict has drawn Western recruits to groups like ISIS. The UK Foreign Office said it is seeking further information from Turkish authorities.

The U.S. Department of Justice has indicted FedEx on 15 counts related to allegedly knowingly shipping controlled substances for illegal online pharmacies since 2004, despite warnings from the DEA, FDA and Congress. FedEx maintains its innocence, invoking the "common carrier" legal exception that shields companies from liability for contents they unknowingly transport. The case raises broader questions about corporate criminal liability and whether such prosecutions serve justice or primarily generate government revenue through settlements.

Kenyans used social media hashtag #147notjustanumber to honor victims of the Garissa University College attack, sharing personal stories and photos. The Al-Shabaab assault killed 147 people, mostly Christian students, making it Kenya's deadliest attack since 1998. Churches held emotional Easter services under armed guard as authorities identified one attacker as a Kenyan official's son.

Swedish photographer Johan Bavman documented fathers taking extended parental leave under Sweden's generous policy, which grants 480 days of leave with 60 "daddy months" reserved specifically for fathers. Bavman aimed to portray realistic experiences of stay-at-home dads, avoiding "superdad" stereotypes, as part of a planned exhibition and book featuring 60 fathers.

President Obama told The New York Times he remains "absolutely committed" to preserving Israel's military edge over Iran, pledging U.S. support if Israel is attacked. His remarks come amid criticism from Netanyahu and Republicans over the nuclear framework deal reached with Iran, which reduces centrifuges and enrichment capacity in exchange for sanctions relief. Final negotiations are set to continue until June 30.

Indiana's new Religious Freedom Restoration Act has sparked controversy over its potential use to justify discrimination against gay people, part of a broader debate stretching back to the 1993 federal RFRA. Twenty states now have similar laws, but experts say successful claims under them are rare and have mostly benefited religious minorities rather than Christian groups, as illustrated by cases involving eagle feathers, sacramental tea, kosher meals, a ceremonial sword, and church zoning disputes.

Five Chinese feminist activists detained ahead of International Women's Day face possible charges of "assembling a crowd to disturb public order," which could bring up to five years in prison. Their detention has sparked international criticism, including from Hillary Clinton, and protests in cities like Hong Kong under the "free the five" campaign. Prosecutors were expected to decide by Monday whether to formally pursue the charges.

Twenty years after her death, Selena's family is creating a hologram-like digital version of the late Tejano star called "Selena the One," using technology from Nevada-based Acrovirt LLC. The project aims to release new songs and videos, collaborate with current artists, and go on tour by 2018, with an Indiegogo campaign launching April 16 to help fund it.

Michele Bachmann compared President Obama's Iran nuclear deal to the Germanwings co-pilot who deliberately crashed a plane, calling Obama a "deranged pilot" flying the nation into destruction. The Facebook comment drew widespread backlash, with critics calling it inappropriate and disrespectful. Bachmann has previously urged Obama to bomb Iranian nuclear facilities, including during a 2014 White House Christmas party.

Ryan Gosling's directorial debut "Lost River," booed at Cannes and panned by critics, is set in a decaying Detroit that Gosling says was the film's true inspiration. He began the project by filming the soon-to-be-demolished Brewster-Douglass Projects before realizing he was making a movie. Gosling says the film aims to show both Detroit's dereliction and its simultaneous resilience and rebirth.

Yahya Rashid, 19, was charged with terror offenses after being detained at Luton airport upon returning from Istanbul. The London man faces charges of preparing and assisting acts of terrorism between November 1 and March 31. He was due to appear in Westminster Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

Mötley Crüe's Vince Neil botched "The Star-Spangled Banner" at a Las Vegas Outlaws game this week, joining a long history of memorable national anthem performances. Whitney Houston's Super Bowl XXV rendition set the gold standard, while Roseanne Barr's 1990 performance drew boos and presidential condemnation. Jimi Hendrix's 1969 Woodstock version and Michael Bolton's forgotten-lyrics attempt in 2003 round out the anthem's most notorious moments.

Photographer Jeff Gusky has documented nearly 2,000 WWI-era graffiti inscriptions left by soldiers in an underground quarry city near Naours, France, rediscovered after the land changed hands in 2013. The writings, mostly from Australian and British troops with some Americans, include names and hometowns, offering a poignant human record of men who sheltered there before facing nearby battles like the Somme.

The Palestinian Authority formally joined the International Criminal Court on Wednesday, becoming its 123rd member and giving the court jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories. The move follows a preliminary ICC examination opened in January into possible war crimes, which Israel and the United States have strongly opposed, arguing Palestine is not a state eligible for membership. Rights groups welcomed the accession as a step toward accountability.

Anthony Ray Hinton, 58, was released Friday after nearly 30 years on Alabama's death row for two 1985 murders he says he didn't commit. Charges were dismissed after firearms experts determined the gun linked to the killings didn't match evidence, and prosecutors declined to retry the case. His attorney, Bryan Stevenson of the Equal Justice Initiative, cited race, poverty and prosecutorial indifference as factors in the "textbook example of injustice."

Most Americans receive tax refunds averaging nearly $3,000, and free filing software has made the process easier, leaving taxpayers with positive feelings about Tax Day despite the system's complexities. This "happy ending" effect, similar to psychological findings about colonoscopy patients, masks deeper unfairness in the tax code, which burdens dual-income married couples and wage earners while allowing the wealthy to minimize taxes on capital gains. Service providers profit from this dynamic by offering free filing while upselling additional services once refunds are secured.

Jordan Spieth maintained his dominant lead at the Masters after a steady third round, finishing four shots ahead heading into Sunday despite a late double bogey. Tiger Woods, Phil Mickelson, Justin Rose and Rory McIlroy all made moves up the leaderboard but could only cut one shot from Spieth's advantage. Woods, evoking memories of Nick Faldo's 1996 comeback, insisted a final-day collapse remains possible.

Liana Barrientos, 39, pleaded not guilty to charges of filing false marriage license applications as part of an alleged immigration scam involving 10 marriages between 1999 and 2010. Prosecutors say she married eight men simultaneously at one point, with several husbands filing for permanent residency shortly after their weddings. She faces up to four years in prison if convicted, with her next court date set for May 18.

Memories Pizza in Walkerton, Indiana, became the center of controversy after owners said they would refuse to cater a same-sex wedding, citing religious beliefs under the state's new Religious Freedom Restoration Act. The restaurant faced boycott calls, vulgar reviews and a threat to burn it down, prompting a police investigation, but supporters raised over $842,000 via GoFundMe. The owners say they are still weighing the cost of their stand.

Vijay Chokalingam, brother of actress Mindy Kaling, revealed he posed as a black applicant to gain admission to medical school, later planning a book about the experience.
